post.title: Forking a 7 MB Terminal: Streaming My tmux Session to Any Browser in 354 Lines of Bun
post.description: I forked crynta's 7 MB Tauri + Rust AI terminal and added a 354-line Bun bridge that streams a live tmux session to my phone over Tailscale.
post.excerpt: Terax is crynta's AI-native terminal built on Tauri 2 and Rust, about 7 to 8 MB on disk by the project's claim. I forked it and prototyped a zero-dependency Bun bridge that mirrors a persistent tmux session to any browser on my Tailscale mesh. Verified end-to-end with two simultaneous clients.
post.content:
First, credit where it belongs: I did not build Terax. Terax is crynta's open-source project, an AI-native terminal with 8,438 stars, Apache-2.0 licensed, that claims about 7 to 8 MB on disk. I forked it as aryateja2106/terax-ai-agentfirst to answer one question: can the same live terminal session follow me from my desk to my phone over my own WireGuard mesh, with zero new dependencies?

The verified answer is yes, in 354 lines of Bun.

## Why 7 MB still matters

AI-native dev environments mostly ship as Electron apps weighing hundreds of megabytes. Cursor, VS Code plus Copilot, all of them bundle a browser to draw a text editor. Terax proves a terminal, an editor, git, and an agentic AI workspace fit in a single-digit-MB native binary.

Two decisions make that possible. Tauri 2 renders through the OS webview (WebKitGTK on Linux, WebView2 on Windows, WKWebView on macOS) instead of shipping Chromium. And the Rust release profile is aggressive: fat LTO, opt-level "s", codegen-units=1, panic=abort, strip=true. The smallness is engineered, not incidental.

One honesty note up front: I did not build and weigh the binary during my fact-check, so the 7 to 8 MB figure is the project's claim, not my measurement.

## What upstream gets right

Terax is a strict two-process architecture. The Rust side owns all OS access: PTY sessions via the portable-pty crate streamed over a Tauri Channel, ripgrep-style search, a full git command surface, an AI HTTP proxy with an SSRF guard, and secrets in the OS keychain via the keyring crate. The React 19 webview never touches the OS directly. Everything is an invoke() call.

The AI layer is BYOK-first: cloud providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Groq, xAI, Cerebras, plus any OpenAI-compatible endpoint) or fully local through LM Studio, MLX, or Ollama. Write and exec tools sit behind in-UI approval cards, and a deny-list refuses secret paths like .env* and .ssh/ on both read and write. No telemetry, no account.

My favorite detail: TERAX.md is simultaneously the in-app agent's project memory and the contributors' living architecture doc. One file, no drift between what the AI reads and what the humans read.

## My problem: the desk is a leash

Terax solved the weight problem. It did not solve mine. A desktop-bound terminal dies when you walk away from the desk. Long-running AI coding agents keep working, but you cannot see or steer them from a phone or a watch.

This fork is R&D for LeCoder, my product. The bridge's SPEC.md names it directly: this is "the realtime multi-device stream MConnect lacked" and the "spine of LeCoder mobile/watch multi-agent multiplexing". If you read my MConnect post, this is the next iteration of the same obsession.

## The seam that makes forks productive

Terax's frontend talks to an abstract four-verb PTY interface: pty_open, pty_write, pty_resize, pty_close. That seam means the whole plan in SPEC.md reduces to "add a second, remote-capable backend, leave the frontend untouched". Clean architecture is what makes a fork worth doing.

The remote backend concept rides on rmux, a tmux-compatible multiplexer written in Rust, on macOS, falling back to plain tmux on Linux via a MUX env var. Same command surface either way, which is itself evidence for why tmux compatibility matters in new tools.

My addition is packages/rmux-bridge: a 354-line Bun WebSocket server with zero npm dependencies (the package.json has no dependencies block at all; xterm assets are vendored), plus a self-contained mobile xterm page with touch support, a key bar for Ctrl, Shift, Alt, Esc, Tab and arrows, pane split buttons, and pane targeting via a ?pane= query param.

## How it works

The obvious route, tmux control mode (-CC), requires a tty and fails from a server process. So the bridge is built entirely from tty-free tmux plumbing:

1. **Attach, never create.** On WebSocket attach the server verifies the session exists. If it does not, it closes with code 1008, "no such session".
2. **Snapshot.** It seeds scrollback with `capture-pane -p -e`, so a new client sees history immediately.
3. **Live stream.** It runs `pipe-pane -O` pointed at a per-connection Unix domain socket that the Bun server listens on, fanning the raw pane bytes out to every connected WebSocket client.
4. **Input.** Keystrokes go back as `send-keys -H`, each byte as its own hex argv element. Every tap on the phone keyboard literally spawns a process with your keystroke as arguments, and it still feels live.
5. **Resize and splits.** Browser resize maps to `resize-window`, and the split buttons map to `split-window`.
6. **Exposure.** A serve.sh helper publishes the port with `tailscale serve`, which makes the WireGuard tailnet the trust boundary.

## Run it yourself

Start the bridge. Default port is 7820, and it binds 0.0.0.0 for tailnet use; set BRIDGE_HOST=127.0.0.1 to keep it local.

```bash
bun run packages/rmux-bridge/src/server.ts
```

Sanity-check the mobile xterm page:

```bash
curl http://127.0.0.1:7820/
```

Run the two-client end-to-end check. One gotcha the README omits, and I hit it myself: the session must exist first, because the bridge attaches and never creates. Without it, the socket closes with 1008.

```bash
rmux new-session -d -s spine-test
PORT=7820 SESSION=spine-test bun run packages/rmux-bridge/scripts/e2e-check.ts
```

When I ran this, the check passed: both WebSocket clients observed the same injected BRIDGE_OK marker on one live session.

To publish it on your tailnet, the serve script wraps tailscale serve and prints the mesh URL. I read the script but did not run it during my fact-check, since it would expose the bridge to my tailnet:

```bash
cd packages/rmux-bridge && bun run serve
```

The desktop app has the standard Tauri flow, documented in the README. I did not execute these during my fact-check either, so treat them as documented, not verified:

```bash
pnpm install && pnpm tauri dev
```

## Honest limitations

- This repo is a fork, not an original project. Upstream crynta/terax-ai built everything I described as the base. My fork adds exactly two commits on a 2026-05-31 base: the rmux-bridge package, about 1,264 lines, and a snapshot commit. I have zero commits in upstream.
- The bridge commit is authored as "Tommy", a local AI agent identity. An agent co-wrote this code under my direction. I work as an Agentic Engineer, this is the workflow, and I would rather state it plainly.
- rmux-bridge is a v0 spike by its own SPEC.md. It has no authentication of its own; the tailnet is the entire trust boundary, and the server binds 0.0.0.0 by default. An auth token is deferred to v1.
- It is a sidecar, not an integrated feature. The Tauri-side backend swap that would wire it into Terax's UI is explicitly out of scope and not implemented.
- It was not merged upstream, and the fork has been behind upstream main since May 31, 2026.
- I verified two browser clients on the dev machine over localhost. I did not test real phone or watch hardware, and I have no latency or throughput numbers for the tailnet path.

## What's next

The interesting follow-up is the one SPEC.md defers: implement the second PTY backend on the Tauri side so Terax's own UI can attach to a remote rmux session through the same four verbs. Then a v1 auth token, then a real phone and watch round-trip over the tailnet. That path is what turns this spike into the spine of LeCoder's mobile multi-agent view.

If you want the terminal, go star [crynta/terax-ai](https://github.com/crynta/terax-ai). If you want the bridge, the fork lives at [aryateja2106/terax-ai-agentfirst](https://github.com/aryateja2106/terax-ai-agentfirst) under packages/rmux-bridge. 354 lines, zero dependencies, bring your own tmux session.
